text: Before you compute a single statistic, you have to know what kind of variable you're looking at. Averaging a column of customer ID numbers will happily return a number, but that number means nothing. This lesson gives you the vocabulary to decide which statistics and charts make sense for which columns, and shows how pandas can help you, and sometimes mislead you.

Categorical variables put each row into a group — region, product category, churned yes or no. Numerical variables are measured or counted quantities where arithmetic is meaningful. Numerical data splits again into discrete, countable with gaps, like orders placed, and continuous, any value in a range, like order value in dollars. A quick test: can a value sit meaningfully between two neighbors? 2.5 orders makes no sense; a 35.25 dollar order does.

Psychologist Stanley Smith Stevens proposed a widely taught ladder of four scales, each adding one property. Nominal: labels with no order, like region — you can count and take the mode, but not a mean. Ordinal: a meaningful order but unequal gaps, like satisfaction ratings — you can rank and take a median, but the gap from low to medium isn't necessarily the gap from medium to high.

Interval: equal gaps but no true zero — temperature in Celsius, where 20 to 25 is the same change as 25 to 30, but 20 degrees isn't twice as hot as 10, because zero is arbitrary. Ratio: equal gaps and a true zero — order value, weight, count of orders — so ratios like twice as much are meaningful. Treat this ladder as a guide to what's defensible, not an absolute law.

In a tiny customer table with customer_id, region, satisfaction, orders, and avg_order_value columns, pandas's dtypes only describe storage, not meaning. customer_id is stored as int64, so calling dot mean on it cheerfully returns 103.0 — a meaningless number, because IDs are really nominal labels. Meanwhile satisfaction is stored as plain text, so pandas has no idea that low is less than medium is less than high.

For a nominal column, counts are the honest summary — value_counts on region gives East 2, West 2, North 1. For an ordinal column, tell pandas about the order explicitly with pd.Categorical, passing categories equals low, medium, high and ordered equals True. Once it's an ordered categorical, max, min, and sorting respect the ranking instead of sorting alphabetically.

The scale determines which statistics are legitimate and which charts to draw — bar charts of counts suit nominal data, histograms suit continuous data. Machine-learning steps later in the path, like encoding categories, depend on this same distinction. To recap: classify every variable as categorical or numerical, discrete or continuous, and nominal, ordinal, interval, or ratio — don't trust storage types alone. Next, we compute our first real statistics: measures of center.
